---
title: Deep Gaussian Processes
authors:
  - name: Adam Buckley
    affiliations:
      - name: Lancaster University
    email: a.buckley4@lancaster.ac.uk
    roles: writing
    corresponding: true
bibliography: references.bib
abstract-title: Abstract
abstract: |
  Gaussian processes (GPs) provide a non-parametric framework for Bayesian inference, providing predictions with principled and calibrated uncertainty estimates. The expressiveness of a single GP is limited by its kernel, which encodes a fixed notion of smoothness across the entire input space. Deep Gaussian Processes (DGPs) aim to address this limitation by composing multiple GP layers into a hierarchy, allowing the model to learn representations at multiple levels of abstraction while retaining the Bayesian uncertainty quantification of standard GPs. This expressiveness comes at a cost of intractable inference, which leads DGPs to require approximate methods for training.

  This dissertation develops the theory of GPs and DGPs from first principles, derives the variational inference framework needed to make DGP training tractable at scale, and evaluates both model families on two benchmark datasets. We begin from the weight-space view of Bayesian linear regression and build to the function-space perspective of GPs, then show how composing GP layers leads to a non-Gaussian joint distribution and motivates doubly stochastic variational inference.

  Two experiments are carried out: a regression benchmark on the Kin8nm robot kinematics dataset and a binary classification benchmark on the UCI credit card default dataset. On Kin8nm, DSVGP-2L achieves a 10.7% RMSE reduction over the single-layer GP, demonstrating that additional GP depth adds value on non-stationary, compositional target functions. On the credit card task, the GP family matches XGBoost on discrimination (ROC-AUC within $\pm 0.003$) while delivering 4-22$\times$ better probability calibration natively; an important property for regulatory probability-of-default estimation. In both experiments, three-layer DGPs never meaningfully outperform two-layer variants and badly degrade at small data scales, indicating that with the constant-mean hidden-layer architecture used here, additional depth beyond two layers does not translate into gains on these tasks. Architectural refinements such as linear-mean ("skip-connected") hidden layers [@salimbeni_doubly_2017] may relax this conclusion and would be the natural next experiment.
---
